clue.text: Wretched, suffering from a childhood complaint

definitions.meaning: having the spotty infectious disease common among children

explanation.definitionFit: One sense is paltry or mean; the other, literal sense describes a child covered in the spots of that illness.

clue.text: Chips so skilful?

parts.note: Mr Chips is the schoolmaster of Goodbye, Mr Chips, so his skill is that of a teacher

explanation.surface: Is a carpenter (nicknamed Chips) this talented?
explanation.walkthrough: Goodbye, Mr Chips is James Hilton's novel about a beloved schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Expert and accomplished, as befits a schoolteacher from the novel.

clue.text: Approved a party point: EDC caught out '

parts.note: a do is a party

indicators.note: the abbreviation for caught is put out of the group of letters

parts.note: European Defence Community, a 1950s alliance proposal
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A party policy is endorsed: the European Defence Community scheme is caught out.
explanation.walkthrough: EDC (the European Defence Community) minus C gives ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken up or accepted formally, as a motion or proposal is.

clue.text: Chicken feed, Marie Antoinette suggested ?

definitions.meaning: food for a laying hen, read literally
the French queen reputedly told the starving poor to eat cake

explanation.surface: Marie Antoinette proposed feeding the peasants a trifling sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken feed' seems to mean a trifling amount, but a layer is a hen; Marie Antoinette reputedly said 'let them eat cake'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gateau made of several tiers of sponge with filling between.

clue.text: So sound-mixers alter speech in the Ring

definitions.text: So sound-mixers alter speech in the Ring

parts.words: So sound-mixers alter speech in the Ring
parts.note: a device that jumbles a telephone signal makes speech unintelligible this way, and boxers in a ring may also be pictured in a disorderly struggle

explanation.surface: Audio engineers distort the singing in a Wagner opera production.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ring suggests Wagner's opera cycle, but the picture is of speech garbled by a security device and of a disorderly tussle.
explanation.definitionFit: To jumble a signal so eavesdroppers cannot follow it, and also a confused rush or struggle.

clue.text: They burn with fury against standard allotments

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
a standard is a flag
rations are allotted portions

explanation.surface: Protesters rage against flags and allocated plots of land.
explanation.walkthrough: Allotments are British rented garden plots, but here the word means portions.
explanation.definitionFit: Great destructive fires blaze fiercely.

clue.text: A cockfight produced with all speed

parts.note: a main is a match of cockfights

explanation.surface: A bout between gamecocks was staged with great haste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produced' is a link. A main is an old term for a cockfighting contest.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic adverb for at full force or speed.

clue.text: Did work badly-student chucked outside

indicators.note: the word for chucked sits round the student letter

parts.note: to bung is to throw or chuck
L is a learner driver's plate, so a student

explanation.surface: A pupil was thrown out for doing poor work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts BUNGED round L.
explanation.definitionFit: Messed up or made a botch of a job.

clue.text: Cockney doctor's job in London Borough

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the first aitch

parts.note: a doctor's work is making people well

explanation.surface: A Cockney doctor working in a London suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, East Londoners, famously drop their Hs. Ealing is a borough in west London.
explanation.definitionFit: The west London district, home of the famous film studios, is one of the capital's boroughs.

clue.text: Novel introduction to Roman history

definitions.meaning: the opening words of the title of Gibbon's great history of the Roman Empire

explanation.surface: An original opening to a study of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new, but it is Waugh's book; Gibbon's work is The History of the ___ of the Roman Empire.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Waugh's satire is also the start of Gibbon's account of imperial collapse.

clue.text: Blackbird heard in TV puppet act

parts.note: Sooty is a yellow glove-puppet bear from long-running British children's television

indicators.note: signals that the word for act is to be taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a turn is a performer's act on stage

explanation.surface: A dark bird turns up in a children's television puppet show.
explanation.walkthrough: SOOTY is a famous British TV glove puppet; a performer's TURN sounds like TERN.
explanation.definitionFit: This seabird of tropical oceans has dark upperparts, so it is a bird that is black.

clue.text: Cancel article " Sally's Comeback "

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the bun-maker's surname is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: Sally Lunn is a sweet teacake from Bath, named after its supposed baker

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece describing a woman's return is to be scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: A Sally Lunn is a light, sweet teacake from the English city of Bath; Sally is not a woman's outing here.
explanation.definitionFit: To declare void or invalid, as a marriage or contract may be.

clue.text: Rose-lit resort in Portugal

indicators.note: read as a verb, to sort again, so the letters of the first word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A seaside town in Portugal bathed in pink light.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' works twice in the &lit: as the noun for the holiday town and as the verb telling you to rearrange ROSELIT.
explanation.definitionFit: The town on the coast west of Lisbon is a well-known holiday spot of the Portuguese Riviera.

clue.text: Many soon to receive £1 for wool extract

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral fifty, so many

indicators.note: the word for soon takes in the money, holding it inside

parts.note: anon is an old word meaning soon
L for pound and I for one

explanation.surface: Lots of people will soon be paid a pound for a wool product.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped the pound sign. £1 gives L (pound, from libra) and I (one), placed inside ANON.
explanation.definitionFit: The greasy substance obtained from sheep's fleece is used in ointments and cosmetics.

clue.text: One lady maybe languishing in Asia Minor

indicators.note: a lady who is languishing is in a poor way, so her letters are thrown about

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A single woman pines away somewhere in Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' is a link; the definition reads as an ancient kingdom found in Asia Minor.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient kingdom of Croesus lay in western Anatolia, the region also called Asia Minor.

clue.text: Men are near to haul trap back with pole

indicators.note: one signal turns the pair of pieces before it round, read from end to start

parts.note: to drag is to haul
a gin is a snare or trap
S is the south pole

explanation.surface: Workers are close by, hauling a trap back with a pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'near' here means stingy, not close by. One 'back' turns both haul and trap words, with the pole letter added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Near is an old word for mean with money, so men who are near are misers.

clue.text: Theatre cat at length bedded in the garden

definitions.meaning: Gus the Theatre Cat in T. S. Eliot's Old Possum poems has a longer full name
a vegetable grown in garden beds

explanation.surface: A long-serving theatre cat is sleeping in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: In Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats, Gus is short for this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Gus's full name in Eliot is also a spear-shaped vegetable grown in beds.

clue.text: Was in control of newspapers mostly, died sadly

indicators.note: most of the word for newspapers is used, losing its final letter

parts.note: the press is the newspapers collectively

indicators.note: the word died is treated badly, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A man who ran most newspapers died, unfortunately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts PRESS to PRES; 'sadly' gives IDED from DIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaired or held authority over, as a judge over a court.

clue.text: Sweet sound of music near seat of trouble

indicators.note: signals the letters of the two words are put into disorder

explanation.surface: Sweet music played close to a troubled place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of trouble' rearranges NEARSEAT.
explanation.definitionFit: An instrumental serenade, a light and melodious piece of music.

clue.text: He put all other racehorses in the shade

definitions.text: He put all other racehorses in the shade

parts.words: He put all other racehorses in the shade
parts.note: an unbeaten eighteenth-century champion whose name means obscuring the sun

explanation.surface: A champion horse outshone all his rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: The horse, unbeaten in 18 races, inspired the saying 'first, the rest nowhere'. Putting in the shade also hints at the sun being blotted out.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous unbeaten racehorse shares its name with the blotting out of the sun by the moon.

clue.text: Father's half-hearted sales-talk

definitions.note: the 's reads as is, linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: the doubled middle letter is halved, losing one of its pair

parts.note: patter is a salesman's glib talk

explanation.surface: Dad's sales pitch lacks conviction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-hearted' removes one of the two Ts at the heart of PATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for a parent, used in old public-school slang for one's dad.

clue.text: Health-giving cooking device

definitions.meaning: one who gives a health, that is proposes a drink to someone
a kitchen appliance for browning bread

explanation.surface: A kitchen appliance that is good for you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Health-giving' looks like 'beneficial', but read it as one who gives (drinks) a health, a salute with raised glasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who proposes a health with a raised glass, and also a kitchen gadget that browns bread.

clue.text: Weaken chance at casino

definitions.meaning: the roulette bet on odd numbers, in French

explanation.surface: A gambler's luck at the tables fades.
explanation.walkthrough: At roulette, 'impair' is the French name for a bet on the odd numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: To lessen in strength, and the French term for odd numbers at the roulette wheel.

clue.text: Hit back at fat bird

indicators.note: the word for hit is turned round, reading from right to left

parts.note: to lam is to thrash or hit
lard is pig fat

explanation.surface: Someone retaliates against a plump bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns LAM to MAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The common wild duck, the drake with its green head.

clue.text: Tavern widow's farewell

parts.note: the forsaken girl of the folk song There Is a Tavern in the Town sings this goodbye in the chorus

explanation.surface: The goodbye of a widow who keeps a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The chorus of the folk song There Is a Tavern in the Town is a goodbye to kind friends in French.
explanation.definitionFit: A French goodbye, wishing someone to God.

clue.text: Hostile incursions where fleet rides at anchor?

definitions.meaning: roads are a sheltered anchorage, so ships moored there are in the roads

explanation.surface: Raids are launched from where a navy is anchored.
explanation.walkthrough: Roads (or roadstead) is a nautical term for a sheltered stretch of water outside a harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: Raids into enemy land; read as two words, it puts ships inside the anchorage.

clue.text: Support from the French has some military point

definitions.meaning: the French word for a prop or support
a point d'appui is a fixed military rallying point

explanation.surface: French backing comes with a strategic military position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link. A point d'appui is a military base of operations.
explanation.definitionFit: French for a prop or stay, used in English military language for a defended pivot position.

clue.text: Gave up a base to house agent in trouble

indicators.note: the base word holds the rearranged spy inside it

parts.note: a bed is a base, as in a flower bed or the bed of a road

indicators.note: the spy's letters are disturbed and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone surrendered a base used to shelter a spy in difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in trouble' rearranges the spy's letters, and 'to house' places them within the base word.
explanation.definitionFit: Renounced or denied oneself, in the sense of self-denial.

clue.text: Don Quixote looked so sadly out of countenance

definitions.text: Don Quixote looked so sadly out of countenance

parts.words: Don Quixote looked so sadly out of countenance
parts.note: Cervantes's hero was dubbed the Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance, in old translations a face full of regret

explanation.surface: Cervantes's knight appears dejected and out of sorts.
explanation.walkthrough: Old English translations call Don Quixote the Knight of the Rueful Countenance.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorrowfully, with regret, the way the Spanish knight's face was described.

clue.text: Belgian queen's detailed riding style

definitions.note: the 's is is, linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: de-tailed, meaning the word for the riding style loses its final letter

parts.note: astride is sitting with a leg on each side, as on a horse

explanation.surface: The Belgian queen's elaborate way of sitting a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' looks like 'elaborate' but means tail removed. Astrid of Sweden was queen of the Belgians, wife of Leopold III.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swedish princess who married Leopold III became the consort of the Belgian king in 1934.
